Help wanted: I'd like to state IsClosed (s.closedInterior) for s : Simplex k P n. What should be the right generality here?
My current guess is that it should use the same set of type classes as docs#AffineSubspace.closed_of_finiteDimensional (plus an order on the field k), but looking at its proof, I noticed it seems to be not needing the metric on the P, so it is already over-specialized?

The version I currently got type-checked is 

theorem Affine.Simplex.isClosed_closedInterior {V P : Type*}
    [AddCommGroup V] [TopologicalSpace V] [IsTopologicalAddGroup V] [T2Space V]
    [Module ℝ V] [ContinuousSMul ℝ V]
    [AddTorsor V P] [TopologicalSpace P] [IsTopologicalAddTorsor P]
    {n : ℕ} (s : Simplex ℝ P n) :
    IsClosed s.closedInterior

which I guess is weakest possible on V and P. Should I bother generalizing from ℝ? The current proof that uses ℝ is docs#Set.Finite.isClosed_convexHull
I think that a better approach is to generalize the definition fo the volume on a Euclidean space so that it works on an AddTorsor over a EuclideanSpace.
E.g., take the map of the map on the underlying space under v => v +_v p, where p is Classical.choice.
If we want to avoid diamonds, then this instance should replace the current one, otherwise they will conflict.

Is that an advice to the overall topic, where you suggest this instead of using Hausdorff measure?
The problem is I'd like to talk about d-dimensional volume in an n-dimensional space, where n is not equal to d, and it can even be a curve, so you can't necessarily embed the object in a Euclidean space with the same dimension
Now I see the issue, thanks for the explanation. I need to think about it before replying.

Yeah I actually asked myself the same question yesterday and got that conclusion. The current definition does match the volume in Euclidean space when the object is "flat" and measured in its own span, so nothing has been lost!
Can't you embed the set into its span, then do what Yury suggests?
A unit circle has a 1-dimensional length of 2pi, but doesn't fit into any 1-dimentional affine subspace.

I also suspect that I need certain completeness hypothesis (example: treating V = ℝ as a ℚ-vector space, the interior of a Simplex ℚ V 1isn't closed)

Weiyi Wang said:

I also suspect that I need certain completeness hypothesis (example: treating V = ℝ as a ℚ-vector space, the interior of a Simplex ℚ V 1isn't closed)

I think if you have some completeness then the stdSimplex will be compact and its image by a continuous function will be closed

That sounds a good idea. Admittedly I didn't think about compactness beyond what is written in the existing code (in metric space compact = closed & bounded). Let me see if I can get compactness in a more general setting

Here is the new version I have got

theorem isClosed_closedInterior {𝕜 V P : Type*}
    [Field 𝕜] [LinearOrder 𝕜] [IsStrictOrderedRing 𝕜] [TopologicalSpace 𝕜]
    [OrderClosedTopology 𝕜] [CompactIccSpace 𝕜] [ContinuousAdd 𝕜]
    [AddCommGroup V] [TopologicalSpace V] [IsTopologicalAddGroup V]
    [T2Space V] [Module 𝕜 V] [ContinuousSMul 𝕜 V] [AddTorsor V P]
    [TopologicalSpace P] [IsTopologicalAddTorsor P] {n : ℕ} (s : Simplex 𝕜 P n) :
    IsClosed s.closedInterior := by -- also IsCompact with the same conditions

The [CompactIccSpace 𝕜] is to get a compact Icc 0 1. Is this good enough?

#37910 is currently in the maintainer-merge queue but @Johan Commelin commented on whether I should extract the cross section object into a new definition. I personally want to bring a conclusion to this long thread, but I also want to clarify that Yan's comment in the PR doesn't represent my sentiment (though I do have something to say below).

My thoughts on the comment in terms of technical details: the cross section object can refer to either the Set of the intersection, or the Affine.Simplex whose closedInterior is the said set. The former doesn't feel like it deserves a new definition, as in Euclidean geometry a plain set can't do much other than volume calculation, which is what being done here. The latter might find more usage in other geometry questions, but it carries its own quirk: for example, one needs to supply a x != 0 (x being the shifting parameter) to its constructor to ensure non-degeneracy of the simplex. This then unnecessarily add more case splitting to the volume calculation. Because of these, I am reluctant to add a new definition.

If it turns out that there is a better way to make the definition and that I should do that, I wish I can have a reviewer that follows up quickly with the review. The whole review process made me question the premise "breaking code into many small PRs makes review faster": every of my PR had to rotate through different reviewers, and each of them needed to learn the context. It would be great if there is a dedicate reviewer who can commit some time to this thread.

Any thoughts?
